title: This change makes /grill-me SO MUCH BETTER
summary: Matt Pocock announces a significant redesign of his Grill Me skill: instead of grilling the user one question at a time, it will grill in batches - rounds of questions. He explains the failure mode that motivated this: near the end of a grilling session the skill would ask a long series of yes/no confirmation questions (do you agree with this recommendation?) that each required a full round-trip to the model provider, wasting time and preventing users from batch-answering. Asking all questions at once fails too, because questions have dependencies - the answer to one can change the next. The solution is rounds: round one asks Q1-Q4 together, the user answers all at once (great for dictation users), and round two takes those answers and asks the follow-ups. The trade-off is slightly more reading per round, but less waiting, fewer context switches, and the ability to run multiple grilling sessions in parallel.
what_you_learn: You learn how to design interactive LLM workflows as batched rounds rather than sequential single questions: a concrete pattern for minimizing model round-trips while respecting dependencies between questions. Directly applicable to building interview, requirements-gathering, or clarification agents.

skills.name: Human-in-the-Loop Collaboration
skills.description: The human stays the driver of the grilling session, answering rounds while the skill orchestrates the questions.

skills.name: Prompt Engineering
skills.description: Reducing wasted model provider round-trips, especially for low-value yes/no confirmation questions.

skills.name: Context Engineering
skills.description: Batching answers so users - especially dictation users - answer multiple questions in one flow with less waiting.

skills.name: Agent Skill Design
skills.description: Iterating on agent skills based on observed failure modes and user modifications, and letting users override via global config.

learnings.title: Grill Me is changing from one-question-at-a-time to batched rounds
learnings.detail: Matt previews the next version of his Grill Me skill: instead of grilling one question at a time, it grills in batches. Round one might ask Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 together, the user replies to all of them, and round two takes those answers and asks the follow-up questions. He calls this about as concurrent as the interaction can get.

learnings.title: The failure mode: end-of-session streaks of yes/no questions
learnings.detail: Grill Me had a weird failure mode where, at the end of a grilling session, it would ask a bunch of questions in a row that were all effectively yeses - yes, I agree with your recommendation. Each of these still cost a full model-provider round-trip: send the request, wait for the response, only then ask the next question. Pure wasted time for zero information gain.

learnings.title: Dictation makes batch answering strictly better
learnings.detail: Matt uses dictation constantly, so if he can see several questions on screen at once he can just dictate out answers to all of them. A single-question-at-a-time design forces him to wait and dictate one short answer per round-trip - especially stupid, as he puts it, given how dictation works.

learnings.title: Users were already hacking around it by asking for all questions at once
learnings.detail: Loads of people were modifying Grill Me themselves to say ask me all the questions at once instead of one by one to get around the round-trip waste. But asking all questions at once fails for a real reason: questions have dependencies between them - the answer to one question might change what the next question should be.

learnings.title: One-by-one questioning only exists to serialize dependencies
learnings.detail: Asking questions one by one gets around the dependency problem by forcing a sequence - it becomes a discussion where each answer shapes the next question. That correctness comes at the cost of latency and context switching, which is why the rounds design is a middle ground rather than a return to full batching.

learnings.title: Rounds of questions: independent questions share a round, follow-ups land in the next
learnings.detail: The design: round one asks Q1-Q4, the user replies to all, and round two takes the answers from the previous round and asks the next follow-ups (Q4, Q5, Q6, for example). Intra-round questions must be independent; dependency chains are expressed across round boundaries. This preserves the discussion-like correctness of sequential grilling while batching the round-trips.

learnings.title: The trade-off: more reading, but faster and parallelizable
learnings.detail: Batch rounds mean the user does a little more reading to understand each question in turn, but it is faster overall and means less context switching - particularly valuable when you run multiple grilling sessions in parallel. Matt had been trying the rounds version all week and found it solves a big issue with Grill Me.

learnings.title: Skills are user-owned: override via global config or edit the skill
learnings.detail: Matt notes that if you do not like the change you can modify your global CLAUDE.md (captioned as claw.md) or modify the skill itself to use the old one-question-at-a-time version. The takeaway for skill authors: ship the better default, but leave users a supported escape hatch since skills live in user-controlled config.

key_points: Sequential questioning burns a model round-trip per question - even for yes/no confirmations.
All-at-once questioning breaks because answers create dependencies between questions.
Rounds are the middle ground: independent questions in one round, follow-ups in the next.
Batch rounds are a gift for dictation users - answer everything on screen in one flow.
Slightly more reading per round buys you speed and parallel grilling sessions.
Users were already patching Grill Me themselves - good skill authors notice and ship the fix.
Do not like the new default? Edit your global CLAUDE.md or the skill itself.
